title: Longest Strict Climb Then Descent
statement:
A hiking app records an elevation profile as an array elev. A ridge is a contiguous stretch elev[i..j] of at least 3 points that rises strictly to a single top and then falls strictly. In other words, there is a top index p with i < p < j, every step from i to p goes strictly up, and every step from p to j goes strictly down.

Return the length of the longest ridge, or 0 if there is none. Flat steps (equal neighbours) break a ridge.

examples.why: 1, 4, 7, 6, 2 climbs to 7 and falls back. It cannot include the 3 before it (that step goes down) or the second 2 (a flat step).
It only climbs. A ridge needs at least one step down after the top.
The flat 4, 4 splits the profile. 1, 4 has no descent and 4, 2 has no climb; only 2, 6, 3 is a ridge.

hints: A ridge is a strict climb followed directly by a strict descent. Where must every ridge start, and where does its top sit?
From a starting point, walk up while values rise, then walk down while they fall. If both walks moved at least one step, you found a ridge. Where should the next search start?

One pass: count the current run of up-steps and the run of down-steps that follows it. Reset both counts on a flat step, or when a climb starts after a descent. Whenever both counts are positive, up + down + 1 is a ridge length.

explain.intuition:
Any ridge is an up-run glued to a down-run. So the only thing you need to know at each step is how long the current up-run was and how long the down-run after it is so far. When both are positive, the stretch from the foot of the climb to here is a ridge of length up + down + 1.

The counts reset in two situations. A flat step ends everything. A step up that comes right after a descent means the old ridge is over and a new climb begins at the bottom of that valley, so the valley point is shared: [1, 3, 1, 3, 1] holds two ridges of length 3, not one of length 5. This is a single pass with O(1) memory, and the same as moving a left pointer to the foot of each new climb.
steps: For each i from 1: if the step is flat, or it goes up while down > 0, reset up = down = 0.
If the step goes up, add 1 to up; if it goes down, add 1 to down.
pitfalls: Counting a pure climb or a pure descent as a ridge. Both parts must have at least one step.
Letting a flat step continue a ridge, as in [1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1].
Starting a new ridge after the valley point instead of at it. The bottom of a valley is the foot of the next climb.

solutions.title: Walk from every start
solutions.idea: From each index, climb as long as values rise, then descend as long as they fall. Keep the longest walk that did both.

solutions.title: One pass with up and down counters
solutions.idea: Track the length of the current climb and the descent after it. Reset on a flat step or when a new climb starts after a descent.

followups: Return the start and end index of the longest ridge, earliest on ties.
Allow flat steps at the top only (a plateau summit). What changes in the counters?
